result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.enumerate_trails()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Enumerate all trails (walks with distinct edges) from source to target. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L31638-L31775){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.enumerate_trails( source, target, max_trails=1000, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Enumerate trails](/assets/graphs/enumerate-trails.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed path A, B, C, D with a loop B, E, F back to B. Both trails from A to D are returned: one goes around the loop (teal) and visits B twice, which a trail allows because no edge repeats; the other is the plain path (accent color)." width="100%"} Returns the actual sequences of nodes for each trail. A trail is a walk where all edges are distinct, though nodes may repeat, so a trail can loop through a node more than once as long as it never reuses an edge. Each trail ends the first time it reaches `target=`. This is the listing counterpart of `count_trails()`. Use it when you need to inspect the routes themselves, for example to: - see which detours make the trail count larger than the simple-path count - collect candidate routes for redundant routing or edge-covering tours - summarize route lengths, or check which nodes are revisited On a directed graph edges are only followed in their own direction; on an undirected graph each edge can be crossed in either direction, but only once. Trails are returned in the order the depth-first search finds them, as lists of node labels (nodes without a label appear as their ID converted to a string). Because the number of trails can grow exponentially, results are capped at `1000` by default. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the trails start from, given as an integer node ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the trails end at, given as an integer node ID or a string label. If it is the same node as `source=`, the result is a single one-node trail. [max_trails]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1000]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of trails to return. Default is `1000`. Once this many trails have been found the search stops and the partial list is returned, so a result of exactly `max_trails=` trails may mean more exist. If `None`, every trail is returned, which can take a very long time and a lot of memory on all but small graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of trails, where each trail is a list of node labels from source to target (both inclusive). If the limit is reached, only the first `max_trails=` trails found are returned. Returns an empty list if `target=` cannot be reached. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or target node not found in graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Same enumeration as `count_trails()`, but every trail is materialized as its full node sequence, which changes the memory picture entirely: even a modest $1{,}000$ trails at $50$ nodes apiece is several megabytes of Python lists, and the counts explode faster than the graph size does, so `max_trails=` must almost always be set to something sane. Because edges are unique but nodes are not, a returned trail can revisit nodes freely, which is exactly what makes trails useful for reasoning about redundant routing, network vulnerability, or edge-covering tours where the walker may pass through a hub several times. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Unlike `count_trails()`, this returns the actual node sequences, so on a triangle we get back both routes from `A` to `C` explicitly: ::: {#6c55c1c0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.enumerate_trails("A", "C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'C'], ['A', 'B', 'C']] ``` ::: ::: Listing the trails shows how they differ from simple paths. In this directed graph the loop `B -> E -> F -> B` produces a second trail that visits `B` twice: ::: {#d6d35322 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("B", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "B"), # Loop back to B ] ) ) graph.enumerate_trails("A", "D") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [['A', 'B', 'E', 'F', 'B', 'C', 'D'], ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']] ``` ::: ::: `max_trails=` bounds how many trails are collected, which matters once a graph is large enough that enumerating every trail would be expensive. Between these two members of the karate club network far more than 100 trails exist, so exactly 100 come back: ::: {#1f4ae95c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} G = ec.karate_club() node_ids = list(G.get_node_ids(limit=None)) trails = G.enumerate_trails(source=node_ids[0], target=node_ids[-1], max_trails=100) len(trails) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 100 ``` ::: ::: With the returned trails in hand, it's easy to summarize how their lengths vary: ::: {#7b4479a2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} lengths = [len(trail) - 1 for trail in trails] # -1 to count edges, not nodes # (shortest, longest) trail length found, in edges (min(lengths), max(lengths)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (4, 67) ``` ::: :::
